nodes.label: Link Layer
nodes.rationale: Transfers a datagram from one node to a physically adjacent node over a wired or wireless link. Services include framing, link access, reliable delivery between adjacent nodes, flow control, error detection and correction, and half- or full-duplex transmission.

nodes.label: Link-Layer Frame
nodes.rationale: Layer-2 packet that encapsulates a datagram and adds a header and trailer so the link can carry it to the next physically adjacent node.

nodes.label: Network Interface Card
nodes.rationale: Host link layer is implemented on-chip or in a NIC that also implements the physical layer, attaches to the host bus (for example PCI), and combines hardware, software, and firmware.

nodes.label: Error Detection
nodes.rationale: EDC bits protect data D. Detection is not 100 percent reliable; a larger EDC field yields better detection. Causes include signal attenuation and noise. The receiver may request retransmission or drop the frame.

nodes.label: Error Correction
nodes.rationale: Receiver identifies and corrects bit errors without retransmission.

nodes.label: Parity Checking
nodes.rationale: Single-bit even or odd parity detects single-bit errors by comparing the parity of received data bits with the received parity bit.

nodes.label: Two-Dimensional Parity
nodes.rationale: Row and column parity detect and correct a single-bit error without retransmission.

nodes.label: Internet Checksum
nodes.rationale: Review of transport checksum (section 3.3): one's complement sum of 16-bit words over a UDP segment including header fields and IP addresses. Equal checksums do not prove the segment is error-free.

nodes.label: Cyclic Redundancy Check
nodes.rationale: Sender chooses r CRC bits R so that D followed by R is divisible by generator G (mod 2). A nonzero remainder at the receiver means an error. Detects all burst errors shorter than r+1 bits. Used in Ethernet and 802.11 WiFi.

nodes.label: Multiple Access Protocol
nodes.rationale: Distributed algorithm that decides when nodes may transmit on one shared broadcast channel. Coordination uses the channel itself; there is no out-of-band channel. A collision occurs if a node receives two or more signals at once.

nodes.label: Point-to-Point Link
nodes.rationale: Dedicated link between two nodes, such as a host and an Ethernet switch, or PPP dial-up access.

nodes.label: Broadcast Link
nodes.rationale: Shared wire or medium: old-school Ethernet, upstream HFC, 802.11 wireless LAN, and 4G/5G or satellite radio.

nodes.label: Channel Partitioning MAC
nodes.rationale: Divides the channel into time, frequency, or code pieces and gives each node a piece for exclusive use. Fair and efficient at high load, but wastes delay and bandwidth at low load because idle shares stay allocated.

nodes.label: TDMA
nodes.rationale: Time division multiple access: each station gets a fixed-length slot in each round. Unused slots go idle.

nodes.label: FDMA
nodes.rationale: Frequency division multiple access: the spectrum is split into bands, each station gets a fixed band, and unused transmission time in a band goes idle.

nodes.label: Random Access MAC
nodes.rationale: Channel is not divided. A node transmits at full rate R with no prior coordination. The protocol specifies how to detect collisions and how to recover, typically by delayed retransmission. Efficient when one node is active; collision overhead grows at high load.

nodes.label: Slotted ALOHA
nodes.rationale: Equal slots, synchronized nodes, transmit only at a slot boundary. On collision, retransmit in each later slot with probability p. Maximum efficiency is 1/e, about 0.37, so at best the channel carries useful transmissions 37 percent of the time.

nodes.label: Pure ALOHA
nodes.rationale: Unslotted ALOHA. Success probability is p times (1-p) to the power 2(N-1) because a node must be alone in both the previous and current frame time. Optimum efficiency is 1/(2e), about 0.18, worse than slotted ALOHA.

nodes.label: CSMA
nodes.rationale: Carrier sense multiple access: listen before transmit. If the channel is idle, send the whole frame; if busy, defer. Collisions still happen because propagation delay hides a transmission that has just started. Distance and delay set the collision probability.

nodes.label: CSMA/CD
nodes.rationale: CSMA with collision detection aborts colliding transmissions quickly, cutting channel waste. Detection is easy on wired links and difficult on wireless links. Ethernet uses unslotted CSMA/CD.

nodes.label: CSMA/CA
nodes.rationale: Carrier-sense random access with collision avoidance, used by IEEE 802.11 because collision detection is hard on wireless links.

nodes.label: Binary Exponential Backoff
nodes.rationale: After the m-th collision, Ethernet picks K at random from 0 through 2^m - 1 and waits K times 512 bit times before sensing again. More collisions produce a longer backoff interval.

nodes.label: Taking-Turns MAC
nodes.rationale: Seeks the high-load fairness of channel partitioning and the low-load efficiency of random access. Nodes take turns, and a node with more to send may hold the turn longer. Realized by polling or token passing.

nodes.label: Polling
nodes.rationale: A centralized controller invites other nodes to transmit in turn. Used with simple devices, including Bluetooth. Costs are poll overhead, latency, and a single point of failure at the master.

nodes.label: Token Passing
nodes.rationale: A control token is passed sequentially; a node transmits only while it holds the token. Used by FDDI and token ring. Costs are token overhead, latency, and failure if the token is lost.

nodes.label: DOCSIS
nodes.rationale: Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification. FDM separates upstream and downstream channels. A downstream MAP frame assigns some upstream slots by TDM and leaves others for random-access requests that use binary backoff. The CMTS at the cable headend transmits downstream.

nodes.label: MAC Address
nodes.rationale: 48-bit LAN or physical or Ethernet address, burned into NIC ROM and sometimes software-settable. Identifies source and destination on one subnet, unlike a 32-bit IP address. IEEE allocates the space to manufacturers. A flat address is portable across LANs; an IP address is not.

nodes.label: Address Resolution Protocol
nodes.rationale: Each IP node keeps an ARP table of IP address, MAC address, and TTL (typically 20 minutes). If the target MAC is missing, the sender broadcasts an ARP query to FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF; the target replies unicast with its MAC, and the sender caches the mapping.

nodes.label: Next-Hop Link Addressing
nodes.rationale: When A sends to B on another subnet, the IP source and destination stay A and B on every hop, while each link-layer frame uses the MAC address of the next-hop interface. A frames to router R; R reframes to B.

nodes.label: Ethernet
nodes.rationale: Dominant wired LAN technology, from Bob Metcalfe's design, spanning about 10 Mbps to 400 Gbps. Connectionless and unreliable: NICs do not handshake or send ACKs or NAKs. Dropped frames are recovered only if a higher layer such as TCP provides reliable delivery. MAC is unslotted CSMA/CD with binary backoff. Bus topology (one collision domain) gave way to a switched star.

nodes.label: Ethernet Frame
nodes.rationale: Preamble (seven 10101010 bytes plus 10101011) synchronizes clocks. Then 6-byte destination and source MAC addresses, a type field that demultiplexes the network protocol (mostly IP; also Novell IPX or AppleTalk), payload, and CRC. A mismatched unicast destination is discarded; a CRC error drops the frame.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.3
nodes.rationale: Ethernet standards share one MAC protocol and frame format while physical layers differ: copper twisted pair and fiber, including 1000BASE-T, 1000BASE-SX, 1000BASE-LX, and speeds from 2 Mbps through 10, 40, and 80 Gbps.

nodes.label: Ethernet Switch
nodes.rationale: Link-layer store-and-forward device. Transparent and plug-and-play. Each host link is its own collision domain and can run full duplex, so pairs of flows transmit simultaneously. A switch table maps MAC address, outgoing interface, and timestamp. Unknown destinations are flooded; known destinations are forwarded or filtered. Interconnected switches learn the same way. Unlike a router, a switch examines link-layer headers and learns by flooding rather than by a routing algorithm.

nodes.label: Switch Self-Learning
nodes.rationale: On each arrival the switch records the sender MAC and incoming interface. It then looks up the destination: drop if the destination is on the arrival segment, forward on the recorded interface if known, otherwise flood on all other interfaces.

nodes.label: VLAN
nodes.rationale: A single physical LAN is one broadcast domain, so ARP, DHCP, and unknown-MAC floods cross the whole LAN and hurt scale, efficiency, security, and privacy. Port-based VLANs group switch ports into virtual switches with traffic isolation. Membership can also follow endpoint MAC addresses and can be dynamic. Forwarding between VLANs is routing. A trunk port carries multiple VLANs between switches.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.1Q
nodes.rationale: Inserts a 2-byte Tag Protocol Identifier (0x8100) and Tag Control Information (12-bit VLAN ID and 3-bit priority) into an Ethernet frame between switches, then recomputes the CRC. Trunk frames cannot be vanilla 802.1 frames because they must carry the VLAN ID.

nodes.label: VXLAN
nodes.rationale: Ethernet VPN, also called VXLAN. Layer-2 switches at distant sites (for example Sunnyvale and Bangalore) are connected by VTEPs. An Ethernet frame is carried inside a UDP segment inside an IP datagram so a Layer-2 network is stretched over a Layer-3 underlay.

nodes.label: RFC 7348
nodes.rationale: Cited definition of VXLAN as a tunneling scheme that overlays Layer 2 networks on Layer 3 networks and runs over existing infrastructure.

nodes.label: MPLS
nodes.rationale: Multiprotocol label switching inserts a fixed-length label (label, Exp, S, TTL) between the Ethernet header and the IP datagram. Label-switched routers forward on the label only, using an MPLS table distinct from the IP table. The IP addresses remain. Paths may depend on source and destination, enabling traffic engineering and fast reroute over precomputed backup paths. Described as an earlier flavor of generalized forwarding.

nodes.label: Virtual Circuit
nodes.rationale: MPLS borrows the virtual-circuit idea of forwarding on a fixed identifier while still carrying a full IP datagram.

nodes.label: RSVP-TE
nodes.rationale: Entry MPLS router uses RSVP-TE to install MPLS forwarding state at downstream routers. OSPF and IS-IS link-state flooding are extended to carry link bandwidth and reserved bandwidth for MPLS routing.

nodes.label: Datacenter Network
nodes.rationale: Tens to hundreds of thousands of closely placed hosts for e-business, content serving, search, and data mining. Challenges are massive multi-application load, reliability, and avoiding processing, network, and data bottlenecks. Rich switch interconnection gives multiple paths and redundancy. Related services are placed in the same or a nearby rack to limit traffic through higher tiers.

nodes.label: Top-of-Rack Switch
nodes.rationale: Access switch, one per rack of about 20 to 40 server blades, with 100G to 400G Ethernet to the blades. Tier-2 aggregation switches connect about 16 TORs; tier-1 core switches connect about 16 tier-2 switches; border routers leave the datacenter.

nodes.label: Leaf-Spine Topology
nodes.rationale: Two-layer datacenter fabric: leaf switches attach to servers or racks and spine switches interconnect the leaves, providing disjoint multipath routes between racks.

nodes.label: Datacenter Load Balancer
nodes.rationale: Application-layer routing: accepts external client requests, directs work inside the datacenter, and returns results while hiding internal structure from the client.

nodes.label: RoCE
nodes.rationale: RDMA over Converged Ethernet, a datacenter link-layer mechanism for remote DMA. Transport innovations on the same networks include ECN-based DCTCP and DCQCN, plus experiments with hop-by-hop backpressure.

nodes.label: Orion SDN
nodes.rationale: Google SDN control plane for the internal Jupiter datacenter network and the B4 wide-area network. Intradomain routing, iBGP, and traffic engineering run as applications on Orion. CoFlow scheduling provides edge-to-edge flow control for SLAs. OpenFlow signals and monitors switches. The slides note that routing protocols, and partly congestion control, are managed by SDN.

nodes.label: DHCP
nodes.rationale: In the web-request walkthrough, a newly attached host broadcasts a DHCP request inside UDP, IP, and 802.3 Ethernet (destination FFFFFFFFFFFF). The router DHCP server returns the client IP, first-hop router IP, and DNS server name and IP. The reply is forwarded using switch learning.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.rationale: After the first-hop MAC is known, a DNS query for www.google.com is encapsulated in UDP, IP, and Ethernet, switched to the campus router, and routed across Comcast using RIP, OSPF, IS-IS, and/or BGP. The DNS server returns the web server IP address.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Before HTTP, the client opens a TCP socket. A SYN is inter-domain routed to the Google web server; the server replies SYNACK, completing the handshake steps shown. TCP is also the higher-layer reliable delivery that recovers data Ethernet drops.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.rationale: The HTTP request is written into the TCP socket, routed as an IP datagram to www.google.com, and the HTTP reply carrying the web page is routed back and displayed.

nodes.label: PPP
nodes.rationale: Point-to-point protocol cited as the link protocol for dial-up access.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.11
nodes.rationale: Wireless LAN broadcast medium. Uses CRC for error detection and CSMA/CA rather than CSMA/CD because wireless collision detection is difficult. Carrier sensing is harder on wireless than on wire.
